newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU finance ministers revive tax harmonisation.
newsitem.headline: EU finance ministers revive tax harmonisation.

text.p: European Union finance ministers, reviving a controversial issue that has stumped them for years, pledged on Monday to tackle loopholes in national tax regimes which damaged other EU partners.
"We are going to go after tax oases energetically," German Finance Minister Theo Waigel told reporters at the first finance ministers' meeting of this year.
"We believe in tax competition but it must be a fair competition. We need common rules of play," he added.
Europe for years has kicked about the idea of trying to agree common tax rules to prevent people or companies in one country flocking elsewhere in the single market to cash in on lower taxes.

But it has consistently run into fears that EU rules on taxation would take away even more national sovereignty from countries already preparing to give up their own currencies at the launch of European monetary union in 1999.
"This is a subject which has been neglected far too long," Italian Treasury minister Carlo Azeglio Ciampi said at a televised opening of the meeting.

Ministers gave few details, however, of how they planned to make progress on taxation, particularly in the face of likely resistance from Luxembourg, which has built a thriving banking centre, helped by its generous tax regime and secrecy laws.

Waigel, when asked the difference between fair and unfair competition, answered simply, "the word 'un'". He said that while the question of Luxembourg's tax system had been discussed, it was not the only one to have been raised.
French Finance Minister Jean Arthuis told reporters the aim would be to seek rules of good conduct to discourage EU members from competing unfairly with each other.

But these would not be imposed on all EU members through a majority, rather than unanimous, vote. "There is no question of revoking the principle of unanimity," he said, adding that the right to set taxes would remain firmly in national hands.

Luxembourg Prime Minister Jean-Claude Juncker denied his country was blocking efforts to bring tax regimes into line, arguing he favoured harmonisation of all taxes, rather than simply of taxes on savings.

Arthuis said the finance ministers had not discussed a call by France for an informal stability council to co-ordinate economic policies after the launch of monetary union, but said there was growing agreement on the issue.

"There is no dispute," he said, repeating that it would be necessary for the euro-zone to have an informal forum in which to co-ordinate economic policies and represent the single currency to countries outside Europe.

The proposal has come under fire from the Bundesbank which fears the council may be used to undermine the independence of the future European Central Bank, though the German government itself has expressed some support for the idea in the past.

Arthuis reiterated that France supported an independent European Central Bank and wanted the euro to be a credible currency. "I support an independent central bank. It is the case in France right now, it will be the case in the European Union."
Earlier Juncker also said there was no row over the council.
"I've seen that the Bundesbank had a strong reaction, but as far as I could see, the German finance minister did not," he told reporters as he arrived for the one-day talks.
"I can't see there are any reasons for a row at all. We will have this stability council as we had the stability pact," Juncker said.
EU leaders agreed in December on a budget discipline pact to ensure monetary union members keep deficits low after 1999.
